paragraphs.text: If you rent, check your tenancy agreement for the notice period you must give your landlord; in many cases it is a month, but some contracts ask for more. Next, decide whether you will hire a removal firm or move your belongings yourself. Anwar Tasker, who manages a removal company, recommends booking at least four weeks ahead, particularly if you hope to move at the end of a month, when demand is highest. 'Most people want to move on a Friday, so the first slots to disappear are those,' he says. Ask each firm for a written quote and find out whether insurance for breakages is included or costs extra. This is also a good time to sort through cupboards: anything you sell, donate or throw away now is something you will not have to pack, carry or pay to transport.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: Contact your current energy and water suppliers to tell them the date you are leaving, so that you stop being charged from that day. On the day itself, read every meter at both the old and new property and photograph the figures; a dated image is the simplest way to settle a disagreement about a final bill. Do not assume you must stay with the supplier the previous occupant used. You can usually switch once you have moved in, although it may be worth checking whether any early-exit fee applies to a fixed-term deal at your old address. Broadband deserves special attention, because connecting a new line can take two weeks or longer. Arrange it well in advance if you work from home, and keep your mobile data allowance in mind for the first few days.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: However carefully you update your address, some letters will still go to your old home. A paid redirection service, offered by the postal service in many countries, forwards your mail to the new address for a chosen period, often three, six or twelve months. Apply at least a week before moving, since the service does not begin immediately. Redirection should be treated as a safety net rather than a solution, however. Write a list of everyone who sends you post — your bank, employer, pension provider, insurers and any magazine subscriptions — and inform each of them directly. Important documents such as bank cards may not be forwarded at all, for security reasons. It is also sensible to leave your new address with a trusted neighbour, who can pass on anything that slips through.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Soon after you arrive, contact the local council about any local property tax and, where relevant, waste collection; some areas issue recycling bins only on request. Adding yourself to the electoral register at your new address is a separate step in many places, so do not assume the council will do it automatically. Yolanda Prescott, a housing adviser who has helped hundreds of families relocate, says the step people most often postpone is finding a doctor. 'They wait until a child is ill, and then discover the nearest practice is not taking new patients,' she explains. Her advice is to register as soon as you have the keys, and to look for a dentist at the same time, as waiting lists can be long. Parents should contact the education authority early about school places, which are usually allocated by area.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: Pack a single box of essentials to travel with you rather than in the van: phone chargers, medicines, a kettle, basic tools, toilet paper and a change of clothes. Before you leave the old property, walk through every room, check cupboards and the loft, and take photographs to show the condition you left it in, which may help if there is a dispute about your deposit. Hand over all keys and get a receipt if possible. In your first week, update the address on your driving licence and vehicle documents; in some countries failing to do so can lead to a fine. Finally, find out where your nearest pharmacy and supermarket are before you need them. Small preparations like these make the first evenings in a new home far less stressful.
paragraphs.label: E

section.text:
Moving House: A Five-Step Checklist

A. If you rent, check your tenancy agreement for the notice period you must give your landlord; in many cases it is a month, but some contracts ask for more. Next, decide whether you will hire a removal firm or move your belongings yourself. Anwar Tasker, who manages a removal company, recommends booking at least four weeks ahead, particularly if you hope to move at the end of a month, when demand is highest. 'Most people want to move on a Friday, so the first slots to disappear are those,' he says. Ask each firm for a written quote and find out whether insurance for breakages is included or costs extra. This is also a good time to sort through cupboards: anything you sell, donate or throw away now is something you will not have to pack, carry or pay to transport.

B. Contact your current energy and water suppliers to tell them the date you are leaving, so that you stop being charged from that day. On the day itself, read every meter at both the old and new property and photograph the figures; a dated image is the simplest way to settle a disagreement about a final bill. Do not assume you must stay with the supplier the previous occupant used. You can usually switch once you have moved in, although it may be worth checking whether any early-exit fee applies to a fixed-term deal at your old address. Broadband deserves special attention, because connecting a new line can take two weeks or longer. Arrange it well in advance if you work from home, and keep your mobile data allowance in mind for the first few days.

C. However carefully you update your address, some letters will still go to your old home. A paid redirection service, offered by the postal service in many countries, forwards your mail to the new address for a chosen period, often three, six or twelve months. Apply at least a week before moving, since the service does not begin immediately. Redirection should be treated as a safety net rather than a solution, however. Write a list of everyone who sends you post — your bank, employer, pension provider, insurers and any magazine subscriptions — and inform each of them directly. Important documents such as bank cards may not be forwarded at all, for security reasons. It is also sensible to leave your new address with a trusted neighbour, who can pass on anything that slips through.

D. Soon after you arrive, contact the local council about any local property tax and, where relevant, waste collection; some areas issue recycling bins only on request. Adding yourself to the electoral register at your new address is a separate step in many places, so do not assume the council will do it automatically. Yolanda Prescott, a housing adviser who has helped hundreds of families relocate, says the step people most often postpone is finding a doctor. 'They wait until a child is ill, and then discover the nearest practice is not taking new patients,' she explains. Her advice is to register as soon as you have the keys, and to look for a dentist at the same time, as waiting lists can be long. Parents should contact the education authority early about school places, which are usually allocated by area.

E. Pack a single box of essentials to travel with you rather than in the van: phone chargers, medicines, a kettle, basic tools, toilet paper and a change of clothes. Before you leave the old property, walk through every room, check cupboards and the loft, and take photographs to show the condition you left it in, which may help if there is a dispute about your deposit. Hand over all keys and get a receipt if possible. In your first week, update the address on your driving licence and vehicle documents; in some countries failing to do so can lead to a fine. Finally, find out where your nearest pharmacy and supermarket are before you need them. Small preparations like these make the first evenings in a new home far less stressful.
